newsitem.title: USA: Clinton hails apparent death of budget amendment.
newsitem.headline: Clinton hails apparent death of budget amendment.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Thursday said he is pleased that a Republican-backed constitutional amendment requiring a balanced budget seems likely to fail in Congress but said lawmakers must now pass a real balanced budget plan quickly.

"It now seems clear the balanced budget amendment will not pass. I think that is a good thing," Clinton said in a speech to the Business Council. It was his first comment on the issue since a key senator announced on Wednseday he would not back the amendment, apparently denying it the votes needed for passage in the Senate.

"But it must also be clear to the American people that we must make sure that a balanced budget does pass, passes this year and passes as soon as we can reasonably pass it," Clinton said. "We have to now go beyond the constitutional debate to get to the specifics. I am convinced that if we pass a balanced budget plan this year it will moderate interest rates, spur more investment and keep growth going."

Republicans want to amend the Constitution to require a balanced federal budget, a complicated procedure requiring two-thirds support of both houses of Congress and approval of three-quarters of the 50 states. That process had just begun in the Senate when Robert Torricelli, a New Jersey Democrat who controlled the required 67th supporting vote, announced on Wednesday he would vote against.

Opponents like Clinton say such an amendment could jeopardize key social spending programs such as Social Security for the elderly with rigid requirements for cost cutting. They say it is not necessary to tamper with the Constitution to achieve sound budget goals.

Clinton was pressing the latter point with his call for fast agreement with the Republicans, who control both houses of Congress, on the next federal budget plan for the fiscal year beginning in October. That would be the vehicle for proposals to reach a balanced budget by 2002.
Clinton said there were some grounds to argue that the usual business cycle of booms followed by recessions had moderated.

"I think there is some argument for that if you look at the better inventory control, the changing nature of the economy to more service jobs, the nature of gloal competition and technology and the greater sophistication at the Fed," Clinton said.

Underlying economic fundamentals had been good because of the productivity of the American people and their willingness to compete. "We have to continue to do the things that will make it likely that success will prevail for another four years and into the next century."
